what: The Egyptian priest Wenamun, sent to buy cedar for the barque of Amun, haggled for timber with Tjekerbaal, prince of Byblos, who demanded payment and reminded him Egypt no longer commanded the coast.
why: The papyrus account is the classic witness to Egypt's collapse of prestige in the Levant at the end of the New Kingdom; whether it is a report or a literary tale is debated.

sources.cite: Story of Wenamun (Moscow Papyrus 120); summarised in Wikipedia, 'Story of Wenamun'

what: The Queen of Sheba came to Jerusalem with spices, gold and precious stones to test Solomon with hard questions.
why: The story, told in 1 Kings 10 and retold in the Quran and the Ethiopian Kebra Nagast, became the founding legend of the Solomonic dynasty of Ethiopia; no historical evidence of the visit exists.

sources.cite: 1 Kings 10; 2 Chronicles 9; Kebra Nagast; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Queen of Sheba'

what: Shown the treasures of Sardis, Solon refused to call Croesus the happiest of men and told him to count no man happy until he was dead.
why: Herodotus' tale became a model of Greek wisdom about fortune, though chronology makes a meeting unlikely (Plutarch already noted the objection).

sources.cite: Herodotus, Histories 1.29-33; Plutarch, Solon 27; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Croesus'

what: King Bimbisara of Magadha met the wandering ascetic Siddhartha at Rajagriha and offered him a share of his kingdom; after his awakening the Buddha returned and the king became a lay follower, giving the Bamboo Grove.
why: Magadha's royal patronage gave the early sangha its first monastery and anchored Buddhism in the Ganges heartland; the episode survives only in Buddhist texts.

sources.cite: Pali Canon, Sutta Nipata 3.1 (Pabbajja Sutta); Vinaya Mahavagga; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Bimbisara'

what: Confucius visited the Zhou court to ask the archivist Laozi about ritual, and was told to put away his pride and ambition.
why: Sima Qian's Shiji made the encounter the emblematic meeting of the Confucian and Daoist traditions, but Laozi's historicity and the meeting are both doubted.

sources.cite: Sima Qian, Shiji 63; Zhuangzi; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Laozi'

what: Ostracised and condemned at Athens, the victor of Salamis fled to Persia and, after a year learning Persian, presented himself at the court of the new king Artaxerxes.
why: The king made the man who had defeated his father governor of Magnesia; Thucydides tells the story as the strangest reversal of the age.

sources.cite: Thucydides 1.137-138; Plutarch, Themistocles 27-29; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Themistocles'

what: Brought by his friend Proxenus, the young Athenian Xenophon joined Cyrus' army at Sardis, believing it was bound against the Pisidians rather than against the Persian king.
why: The campaign ended at Cunaxa and produced the Anabasis, Xenophon's account of leading the Ten Thousand home.

sources.cite: Xenophon, Anabasis 3.1; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Anabasis (Xenophon)'

what: Plato visited the tyrant Dionysius I and spoke so freely against tyranny that, by later tradition, he was handed to a Spartan envoy and sold as a slave on Aegina.
why: Plato's three Sicilian visits became the cautionary tale of the philosopher at a tyrant's court; the slave-sale story is late and uncertain.

sources.cite: Diogenes Laertius 3.18-21; Plato, Seventh Letter; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Plato'

what: Philip II summoned Aristotle to Macedon and gave him the Temple of the Nymphs at Mieza as a school for the thirteen-year-old Alexander.
why: The most famous teacher-student pair of antiquity: Alexander carried Homer annotated by Aristotle on campaign and sent him specimens from Asia, by later report.

sources.cite: Plutarch, Life of Alexander 7-8; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Aristotle'

what: Finding Diogenes sunning himself, Alexander asked what he could do for him; Diogenes asked him to stand out of his light.
why: Plutarch and Diogenes Laertius made it the archetype of philosophy facing power; Alexander was in Corinth in 336 but the exchange is anecdote.

sources.cite: Plutarch, Life of Alexander 14; Diogenes Laertius 6.38; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Diogenes'

what: Alexander's envoy Onesicritus found naked ascetics outside Taxila; one of them, Kalanos, agreed to join Alexander's court.
why: Kalanos travelled with the army to Persia and burned himself alive at Pasargadae, the most vivid Greek encounter with Indian asceticism.

sources.cite: Arrian, Anabasis 7.2-3; Strabo 15.1.63-68; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Kalanos'

what: After the Battle of the Hydaspes the wounded Porus, asked how he wished to be treated, answered 'like a king', and Alexander restored and enlarged his kingdom.
why: Porus became Alexander's ally on the eastern frontier; the battle marked the furthest high tide of Macedonian conquest into India.

sources.cite: Arrian, Anabasis 5.19; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Porus'

what: Megasthenes went as Seleucus I's ambassador to the Mauryan court at Pataliputra and described the city, its palisade and its king.
why: His Indica, preserved in fragments by Arrian and Strabo, was the West's main picture of India for centuries.

sources.cite: Arrian, Indica; Strabo 15.1; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Megasthenes'

what: On the eve of battle Hannibal asked for a parley and met Scipio between the two armies with only interpreters; Scipio rejected his peace terms.
why: The next day Scipio won at Zama, ending the Second Punic War and Carthage's power.

sources.cite: Polybius 15.6-8; Livy 30.29-31; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Battle of Zama'

what: Fleeing Carthage, Hannibal reached Antiochus III at Ephesus and offered his services against Rome.
why: Antiochus kept him as adviser but ignored his plans; defeat at Magnesia forced the king to agree to surrender Hannibal, who fled again.

sources.cite: Livy 33.49; Appian, Syriaca 4; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Hannibal'

what: Asked by Scipio who was the greatest general, Hannibal named Alexander, Pyrrhus and himself, and said that had he beaten Scipio he would have put himself first.
why: Livy reports the conversation from Claudius Quadrigarius and doubts it; it survives as the classic exchange between great rivals.

sources.cite: Livy 35.14; Plutarch, Flamininus 21; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Scipio Africanus'

what: The Indo-Greek king Menander questioned the monk Nagasena on the self, rebirth and karma until, by the text's account, he was converted.
why: The Milindapanha records the dialogue; Menander is real, but the conversation is a literary framing of Buddhist doctrine.

sources.cite: Milindapanha; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Milinda Panha'

place: Yuezhi court north of the Oxus
what: After ten years as a Xiongnu captive, the Han envoy Zhang Qian reached the Yuezhi in Bactria and asked them to return east as allies against the Xiongnu; the king, settled and prosperous, declined.
why: The mission failed diplomatically but Zhang Qian's report on Ferghana, Bactria and Parthia opened Han interest in the routes later called the Silk Road.

sources.cite: Sima Qian, Shiji 123; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Zhang Qian'

what: Li Ling, the Han general who had surrendered to the Xiongnu, visited the captive envoy Su Wu at his sheep-herding exile by the 'North Sea' to urge him to submit; Su Wu refused.
why: Su Wu's nineteen years of loyalty made him a Chinese byword for fidelity; he returned to Chang'an in 81 BCE.

sources.cite: Ban Gu, Hanshu 54; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Su Wu'

what: The aged king Tigranes came to Pompey's camp, laid his diadem at his feet and was raised up and crowned again as a client of Rome.
why: The submission ended Armenia's brief empire and set the Roman-Armenian frontier for generations.

sources.cite: Plutarch, Pompey 33; Cassius Dio 36.52; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Tigranes the Great'

what: Cleopatra, in conflict with her brother Ptolemy XIII, had herself smuggled into the palace at Alexandria to meet Caesar, who had arrived pursuing Pompey.
why: Caesar backed her in the Alexandrian war and the alliance produced Caesarion; Plutarch's bedding-sack detail is the famous part of the story.

sources.cite: Plutarch, Caesar 49; Cassius Dio 42.34; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Cleopatra'

what: Summoned by Antony to answer for her conduct, Cleopatra sailed up the Cydnus to Tarsus in a gilded barge and entertained him on board.
why: Their political and personal partnership ended at Actium in 31 BCE and with Egypt's annexation by Rome.

sources.cite: Plutarch, Antony 26; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Antony and Cleopatra'

what: Visiting the Han court, the Xiongnu chanyu Huhanye asked for a consort, and the palace lady Wang Zhaojun was given to him in marriage.
why: The heqin match sealed decades of peace on the northern frontier, and Zhaojun became one of the Four Beauties of Chinese legend.

sources.cite: Hanshu 94; Hou Hanshu 89; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Wang Zhaojun'

what: Jesus came to John at the Jordan and was baptised by him.
why: Attested in all four gospels and accepted by most historians, the baptism marks the start of Jesus' public ministry.

sources.cite: Mark 1:9-11; Matthew 3; Luke 3; John 1; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Baptism of Jesus'

what: Three years after his conversion Paul went up to Jerusalem to visit Cephas (Peter) and stayed with him fifteen days.
why: Paul's own letter is the earliest first-hand testimony of contact between the apostles; their later quarrel at Antioch shaped the gentile mission.

sources.cite: Paul, Galatians 1:18; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Paul the Apostle'

what: After calling three times at his thatched cottage, Liu Bei met the young recluse Zhuge Liang, who laid out the Longzhong Plan for dividing the realm into three.
why: Zhuge Liang became Liu Bei's chancellor and the plan foreshadowed the Three Kingdoms; Zhuge's own memorial recalls the three visits.

sources.cite: Chen Shou, Records of the Three Kingdoms; Zhuge Liang, Chu Shi Biao; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Zhuge Liang'

what: Valerian went to negotiate with Shapur near Edessa and was seized, the first Roman emperor taken prisoner by a foreign enemy.
why: Shapur carved the scene into the cliffs at Naqsh-e Rostam; Valerian died in Persian captivity.

sources.cite: Shapur I, Res Gestae Divi Saporis (ŠKZ); Zosimus 1.36; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Valerian (emperor)'

what: The young rhetoric professor Augustine arrived in Milan and went to hear Bishop Ambrose preach, at first for his style.
why: Ambrose's allegorical reading of scripture dissolved Augustine's objections; Ambrose baptised him at Easter 387.

sources.cite: Augustine, Confessions 5.13-14; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Augustine of Hippo'

what: The Byzantine embassy of Maximinus, with the historian Priscus, reached Attila's wooden palace and dined at his table.
why: Priscus' eyewitness account is the only close description of Attila and his court.

sources.cite: Priscus, fragments in Constantine VII's Excerpta de legationibus; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Priscus'

what: Pope Leo, with two senators, met Attila in northern Italy and persuaded him to withdraw.
why: The Huns turned back; Leo's credit for it grew into legend (Raphael painted Peter and Paul in the sky), though plague and supply also mattered.

sources.cite: Prosper of Aquitaine, Chronicle; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Pope Leo I'

what: Emperor Wu asked how much merit his temple-building had earned; Bodhidharma answered 'none at all', and left for the north.
why: A founding story of Chan (Zen); it first appears centuries after the fact and is regarded as legend.

sources.cite: Blue Cliff Record, case 1; Anthology of the Patriarchal Hall (952); summarised in Wikipedia, 'Bodhidharma'

what: Travelling with his uncle's caravan to Syria, the boy Muhammad was recognised by the Christian monk Bahira as a future prophet.
why: Told in the early Sira and in Christian polemic alike, the story is regarded as legend.

sources.cite: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Bahira'

what: Ono no Imoko presented a letter from Prince Shotoku addressed 'from the Son of Heaven where the sun rises to the Son of Heaven where the sun sets', which displeased Emperor Yang.
why: Japan's first well-recorded embassy to China opened the flow of Chinese learning, Buddhism and statecraft to Asuka Japan.

sources.cite: Book of Sui 81; Nihon Shoki; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Ono no Imoko'

what: Muslim refugees from Mecca, led by Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, were received by the Christian king (Najashi) of Aksum, who refused Quraysh demands to hand them back after hearing Ja'far recite the Quran.
why: The First Hijra gave the early Muslim community its first refuge; the dialogue is preserved in early Islamic biography.

sources.cite: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Migration to Abyssinia'

what: The king of Gaochang detained the pilgrim Xuanzang, begging him to stay as his teacher, and released him only after a hunger strike, with letters and escorts for the road west.
why: Qu Wentai's support carried Xuanzang across Central Asia to India.

sources.cite: Huili, Biography of the Tripitaka Master; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Xuanzang'

what: Patriarch Sophronius surrendered Jerusalem to the caliph Umar in person; tradition says he showed him the Temple Mount and Umar declined to pray in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre.
why: Jerusalem passed to Muslim rule; the meeting is reported by later Byzantine and Arab chroniclers, and many details (the 'Covenant of Umar') are later embellishment.

sources.cite: Theophanes the Confessor, Chronographia; al-Tabari; summarised in Wikipedia, 'First Muslim conquest of Jerusalem'

what: King Harsha received the Chinese pilgrim at Kannauj and convened a great assembly where Xuanzang defended Mahayana doctrine.
why: Xuanzang's record is the main outside description of Harsha's empire; Harsha then opened diplomatic relations with Tang China.

sources.cite: Xuanzang, Great Tang Records on the Western Regions; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Harsha'

what: On his return after sixteen years, the pilgrim who had left China illegally was received by Taizong, who pressed him to take office and asked him to write an account of the West.
why: Xuanzang declined office and translated scriptures; his Records on the Western Regions was the result of the emperor's request.

sources.cite: Huili, Biography of the Tripitaka Master; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Xuanzang'

what: The two greatest Tang poets met in Luoyang and travelled together for a time in Henan and Shandong.
why: Du Fu wrote at least a dozen poems to or about Li Bai; the friendship became a symbol of literary kinship.

sources.cite: Du Fu, poems to Li Bai; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Li Bai'

what: Attacked and driven from Rome, Pope Leo III fled to Charlemagne at Paderborn to seek protection.
why: Charlemagne restored him; on Christmas Day 800 Leo crowned him emperor in St Peter's.

sources.cite: Royal Frankish Annals; Paderborn Epic; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Pope Leo III'

what: The Japanese monk Kukai went to the esoteric master Huiguo, who greeted him as long awaited and initiated him into both mandala lineages within months, shortly before dying.
why: Kukai carried the teaching home and founded Shingon Buddhism.

sources.cite: Kukai, Memorial Presenting a List of Newly Imported Sutras; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Kūkai'

what: The Abbasid embassy with Ibn Fadlan reached the Volga Bulgar ruler Almış, who had asked the caliph for teachers of Islam and a fortress.
why: Ibn Fadlan's report is the earliest detailed account of the Volga peoples and of the Rus.

sources.cite: Ibn Fadlan, Risala; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Ahmad ibn Fadlan'

what: Princess Olga of Kiev was received at the Great Palace by Constantine VII, who recorded the ceremonies in his book of court protocol.
why: Olga's baptism and visit foreshadowed the Christianisation of the Rus under her grandson Vladimir.

sources.cite: Constantine VII, De Ceremoniis 2.15; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Olga of Kiev'

what: Otto I's envoy Liutprand came to arrange a Byzantine bride for Otto's son and was insulted, confined, and refused.
why: His bitter Relatio de legatione Constantinopolitana is a famous portrait of the rivalry between the two empires.

sources.cite: Liutprand, Relatio de legatione Constantinopolitana; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Liutprand of Cremona'

what: Excommunicated, Henry IV stood three days in the snow outside Canossa as a penitent until Gregory lifted the ban.
why: 'Going to Canossa' became the byword for submission in the struggle between papacy and empire.

sources.cite: Lampert of Hersfeld, Annals; Gregory VII, Register 4.12; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Road to Canossa'

what: Brought together by Lü Zuqian, Zhu Xi and Lu Jiuyuan debated whether the Way is found by studying things or by searching the mind.
why: The Goose Lake Meeting fixed the split between the Cheng-Zhu and Lu-Wang schools of Neo-Confucianism.

sources.cite: Lu Jiuyuan, Collected Works; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Lu Jiuyuan'

what: Frederick Barbarossa knelt before Pope Alexander III at San Marco and received the kiss of peace.
why: The Peace of Venice ended an eighteen-year schism and Frederick's attempt to rule Italy by force.

sources.cite: Romuald of Salerno, Chronicon; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Treaty of Venice'

what: The aged philosopher Ibn Rushd asked to meet the teenage mystic Ibn Arabi, asked him whether illumination agreed with reason, and was answered 'yes and no'.
why: Ibn Arabi tells the story himself in the Futuhat; it stands for the meeting of falsafa and Sufism.

sources.cite: Ibn Arabi, al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Ibn Arabi'

what: Balian came out to Saladin's camp and, threatening to destroy the city and its holy places, negotiated the surrender of Jerusalem with ransom for its people.
why: Jerusalem passed to Saladin on 2 October 1187 without a massacre, which triggered the Third Crusade.

sources.cite: Ernoul; Imad ad-Din al-Isfahani; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Siege of Jerusalem (1187)'

what: Saladin's brother al-Adil met Richard in his tent near Lydda, where they ate together and discussed Richard's proposal that al-Adil marry Richard's sister Joan.
why: Richard never met Saladin; talks through al-Adil eventually produced the Treaty of Jaffa (1192) and pilgrim access to Jerusalem.

sources.cite: Baha ad-Din ibn Shaddad, al-Nawadir al-Sultaniyya; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Al-Adil I'

what: Passing through Nishapur with his family, the boy Rumi met the aged Attar, who gave him his Asrarnama and said he would set fire to the world's lovers.
why: Told in later hagiography; the meeting is doubtful but expresses Rumi's debt to Attar.

sources.cite: Dawlatshah Samarqandi, Tadhkirat al-Shu'ara; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Attar of Nishapur'

what: During the Fifth Crusade Francis crossed the lines at Damietta to preach before Sultan al-Kamil, who received him courteously and let him go.
why: Attested by Jacques de Vitry, the visit became a lasting emblem of Christian-Muslim encounter.

sources.cite: Jacques de Vitry, Letters; Historia Occidentalis; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Francis of Assisi'

what: The Daoist master Changchun, summoned across Asia, met Genghis Khan in the Hindu Kush and was asked for the medicine of immortality; he answered there was none, only means of preserving life.
why: Genghis exempted the Quanzhen Daoists from taxes; the journey was recorded by the disciple Li Zhichang.

sources.cite: Li Zhichang, Travels to the West of Qiu Chang Chun; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Qiu Chuji'

what: The wandering dervish Shams of Tabriz met the respected scholar Jalal al-Din Rumi in Konya, and the two withdrew into intense companionship for months.
why: Shams' disappearance turned Rumi into a poet: the Divan-e Shams and the Masnavi followed.

sources.cite: Aflaki, Manaqib al-Arifin; Sultan Walad; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Shams Tabrizi'

what: The papal envoy Carpine witnessed Güyük's enthronement and was given a reply demanding that the Pope and the princes of Europe come to submit.
why: The first European embassy to the Mongols brought back a sober account of them and a letter (still in the Vatican) rejecting Christian claims.

sources.cite: Carpine, Ystoria Mongalorum; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Giovanni da Pian del Carpine'

what: The Tibetan lama Sakya Pandita, summoned by the Mongol prince Köden, met him at Liangzhou and agreed to Tibet's submission.
why: The meeting began the priest-patron relationship between Tibetan lamas and Mongol rulers.

sources.cite: Sakya Pandita's letter to the Tibetans; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Sakya Pandita'

what: The Flemish friar was received by the Great Khan Möngke, and in May took part in a debate before him between Christians, Muslims and Buddhists.
why: Rubruck's report is the fullest medieval European account of the Mongol court.

sources.cite: William of Rubruck, Itinerarium; summarised in Wikipedia, 'William of Rubruck'

what: When the Nizari imam surrendered Maymun-Diz to Hulagu, the astronomer al-Tusi, who had served the Ismailis for decades, came over to the Mongols.
why: Hulagu made him adviser and built him the Maragheh observatory, a high point of medieval astronomy.

sources.cite: Rashid al-Din, Jami al-Tawarikh; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Nasir al-Din al-Tusi'

what: The last Abbasid caliph came out to surrender to Hulagu and was made to reveal his treasure; he was executed days later.
why: The sack of Baghdad ended the Abbasid caliphate in Iraq.

sources.cite: Rashid al-Din, Jami al-Tawarikh; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Siege of Baghdad'

what: Marco Polo, with his father and uncle, reached Kublai's summer capital and entered his service for some seventeen years.
why: His book shaped European ideas of Asia; a minority of scholars doubt how much of it he saw himself.

sources.cite: Marco Polo, Il Milione; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Marco Polo'

what: The Nestorian monk sent west by the Ilkhan Arghun met Edward I in Gascony and gave him communion, proposing a joint crusade against the Mamluks.
why: Bar Sauma also met Philip IV and Pope Nicholas IV; the alliance never materialised.

sources.cite: History of Mar Yahballaha and Rabban Sauma; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Rabban Bar Sauma'

what: Zhou Daguan, with a Yuan embassy, spent a year at Angkor and watched the king ride out in procession with his white parasols and armed women.
why: His Customs of Cambodia is the only eyewitness account of daily life in Angkor.

sources.cite: Zhou Daguan, The Customs of Cambodia; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Zhou Daguan'

what: On pilgrimage, Mansa Musa reluctantly met the Mamluk sultan, refusing at first to kiss the ground before him, and spent so much gold that its value in Cairo fell.
why: The visit, recorded by al-Umari, put Mali on European maps such as the Catalan Atlas.

sources.cite: al-Umari, Masalik al-Absar; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Mansa Musa'

what: Ibn Battuta visited Kilwa and saw its sultan, Abu al-Muzaffar Hasan, give away his own clothes to a beggar.
why: He called Kilwa one of the most beautiful cities; the account documents Swahili coast trade.

sources.cite: Ibn Battuta, Rihla; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Kilwa Kisiwani'

what: The Moroccan traveller was received by the sultan of Delhi, who showered him with gifts and appointed him a qadi.
why: He served eight years before being sent as envoy to China, a mission that went awry.

sources.cite: Ibn Battuta, Rihla; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Ibn Battuta'

what: On his way to Rome for the Jubilee, Petrarch was welcomed in Florence by Boccaccio, his long-time admirer.
why: The friendship joined the two founders of humanism and led Boccaccio toward classical scholarship.

sources.cite: Petrarch, Familiares 11.1; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Giovanni Boccaccio'

what: Ibn Battuta reached the capital of Mali and was received by Mansa Sulayman, complaining of the meagre welcome gift.
why: His account is the main eyewitness description of the Mali court; the capital's site is uncertain.

sources.cite: Ibn Battuta, Rihla; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Sulayman of Mali'

what: Back in Morocco, Ibn Battuta was received by the Marinid sultan Abu Inan, who ordered his secretary Ibn Juzayy to write down his travels.
why: The result was the Rihla, the great travel book of the medieval world.

sources.cite: Ibn Battuta and Ibn Juzayy, Rihla; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Ibn Battuta'

what: On an embassy to Italy in 1373, Chaucer may have met Petrarch at Padua, as his Clerk claims to have learned the Griselda tale from him.
why: No document confirms the meeting; it remains a favourite literary speculation.

sources.cite: Chaucer, Canterbury Tales, Clerk's Prologue; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Geoffrey Chaucer'

what: Timur reproached Hafez for offering Samarkand and Bukhara for a Shirazi beauty's mole; the poet replied that such generosity was why he was so poor.
why: The anecdote appears in Dawlatshah over a century later and is legend.

sources.cite: Dawlatshah Samarqandi, Tadhkirat al-Shu'ara; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Hafez'

what: Lowered over the walls of besieged Damascus, the historian Ibn Khaldun spent weeks in Timur's camp, discussing history and writing him a description of the Maghreb.
why: Ibn Khaldun's autobiography records one of history's great conversations between a conqueror and a theorist of conquest.

sources.cite: Ibn Khaldun, al-Ta'rif; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Ibn Khaldun'

what: After the Battle of Ankara the captured Ottoman sultan was brought before Timur, who treated him at first with courtesy.
why: Bayezid died in captivity in 1403 and the Ottoman state fell into a decade of civil war; the 'iron cage' story is later embellishment.

sources.cite: Ibn Arabshah; Sharaf al-Din Yazdi, Zafarnama; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Battle of Ankara'

what: The Castilian ambassador was received by the aged Timur in a garden palace outside Samarkand.
why: Clavijo's Embajada a Tamorlán is the fullest European picture of Timur's capital, months before the conqueror's death.

sources.cite: Clavijo, Embajada a Tamorlán; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Ruy González de Clavijo'

what: The fifth Karmapa came to Nanjing at the emperor's invitation and performed rites for the emperor's late parents; Yongle gave him the title of Dharma King.
why: The visit set the pattern of Ming patronage of Tibetan lamas.

sources.cite: Ming Shilu; Tibetan accounts; summarised in Wikipedia, '5th Karmapa, Deshin Shekpa'

what: Returning from his third voyage, Zheng He fought the Sinhalese ruler Alakeshvara and carried him captive to Nanjing.
why: The Yongle Emperor released him but installed a new ruler, one of the few times the treasure fleets made war.

sources.cite: Ming Shilu; Mingshi 304; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Zheng He'

what: Months after the conquest, Mehmed II received the monk Gennadios, had him elected patriarch and handed him his staff of office.
why: The investiture set the template for Ottoman rule over Orthodox Christians through their patriarch.

sources.cite: Sphrantzes; Kritoboulos; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Gennadius Scholarius'

what: Sent by Venice at the sultan's request for a good painter, Gentile Bellini spent over a year at Mehmed's court and painted his portrait.
why: The portrait (National Gallery, London) is the most famous Western image of an Ottoman sultan.

sources.cite: Angiolello; Vasari; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Gentile Bellini'

what: Columbus first put his plan of sailing west to the Indies before Isabella and Ferdinand.
why: A commission rejected it, but after years of lobbying the monarchs backed him at Santa Fe in 1492.

sources.cite: Las Casas, Historia de las Indias; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Christopher Columbus'

what: The Portuguese embassy under Rui de Sousa reached the king of Kongo, who was baptised as João I.
why: The baptism began the long Kongo-Portugal relationship and the Christian kingdom of Afonso I.

sources.cite: Rui de Pina, Crónica de D. João II; summarised in Wikipedia, 'João I of Kongo'

what: The Taíno cacique Guacanagarí sent gifts to Columbus and, when the Santa María wrecked on Christmas Day, helped salvage its cargo.
why: Columbus left 39 men at La Navidad in his territory; all were dead when he returned in 1493.

sources.cite: Columbus, Diario (via Las Casas); summarised in Wikipedia, 'Guacanagaríx'

what: The North African jurist al-Maghili came to Gao and answered Askia Muhammad's questions on how a Muslim ruler should govern.
why: His 'Replies' were used by Songhay and later West African reformers, including Usman dan Fodio, to justify jihad against 'mixing' rulers.

sources.cite: al-Maghili, Replies to the Questions of Askia; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Al-Maghili'

what: After hostility at Mombasa, da Gama found a friendly ruler at Malindi who gave him a pilot for the crossing to India.
why: With the pilot's help the fleet crossed the Arabian Sea in 23 days; Malindi became Portugal's ally on the Swahili coast.

sources.cite: Álvaro Velho, Roteiro; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Vasco da Gama'

what: Da Gama was received by the Zamorin, who was unimpressed by his gifts of cloth, hats and honey.
why: Trade talks failed but the voyage proved the sea route to India, and Portuguese violence soon followed.

sources.cite: Álvaro Velho, Roteiro; summarised in Wikipedia, 'Vasco da Gama'

what: On Erasmus' first visit to England, Thomas More took him to Eltham Palace to meet the eight-year-old Prince Henry.
